text:
Some lessons only land when you've failed enough times to stop blaming the team. 😩

In 2020, I asked my team at 1.618 – the architecture and design bureau I'd co-founded, for honest feedback about my leadership.

I was a directive leader back then. My soft skills were basically nonexistent. Five years of chasing results, and I'd burned relationships with almost everyone who worked for me. I wanted to build a teal organization but had no idea how.

So I gave my team the power to decide my fate → And the best thing in the opinion of the team was to get rid of me🤦‍♂️

I left the company I'd built from scratch. 60+ completed projects behind me, and a personal bank debt from a loan I'd taken to cover the team's salaries. The same team that fired me.🤦‍♂️

Eventually, they closed the business within two months.🤦‍♂️


🔁 Different company - SoftServe. A project with a Polish colleague, a team of four. Our very first intro meeting, and he escalated to my manager. The complaint: I was negative, I didn't listen, I kept interrupting.

He was an introvert who needed time to think. I was loud and fast and couldn't sit through his pauses. He couldn't actually share his opinion, because I kept taking the initiative for him.

Same pattern, different company and it took me years to really see it.

🔑 The breakthrough came when I started running real 1-on-1s with every person on my team, every three weeks.

Not status updates like "where are we on your tasks." In the first meeting I told each of them the same thing: this conversation isn't for me. It's for you. It's your space so bring whatever you're carrying: work, life, fears, ideas, doubts - anything. And let's build a friendship.

I ended up spending a huge part of my working time on these conversations. I used to be part manager, part coach, sometimes part therapist.

💡 And for the first time, I saw a different way to influence results. Through personal connection instead of process enforcement. Through individual motivation instead of treating people as interchangeable parts.

The one skill I'd avoided my entire career? Genuine listening - empathy. Meeting people where they are? It turned out to be the one that changes everything.

🤝 Eventually I found my way to Speed and Function. A company where collaboration is the engine. Where soft skills matter more than technical ones, and the culture doesn't just tolerate growth, it demands it.

Now let's run a quick experiment → drop an emoji in the comments that represents how your manager runs one-on-ones with you. 👇
